subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, April 14, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at the outset to associate myself with the sentiment expressed by the hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) when he delivered his statement to the House, in which he voiced his regret that the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is not able to be in his place in the House and could not be here to present the annual financial statement. I am sure that it would have been a pleasure to. him to announce to the House and the country the successful consummation of the policy of economy and retrenchment which this government has put in force during the past two years. The announcement, however, that the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Robb) was to take the place of the Minister of Finance was received by the people with confidence and assurance, knowing, as they did, that the record of my hon. colleague since he has been in public life would be assurance of the delivery of an able budget speech.
If I may be permitted, Mr. Speaker, I should like to review briefly a few of the steps that have led up to the conditions that
1368	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
obtain in Canada to-day and which have culminated in the announcement of the Acting Minister of Finance that the government have been able to balance their budget and to effect a considerable reduction of the public debt. I will ask hon. members to look back over the period of the last two years, or a little more, during which the present government have been in power. By doing this we will see the many obstacles which the government have had to overcome in arriving at the position indicated by the Acting Finance Minister.
When the government took office we found that the exchange as applied to our dealings with our greatest customer, the United States, was at a discount of from 10 to 12 and sometimes 15 per cent. Conditions generally in Canada were not good. Unemployment was rife in our industrial centres; we found it necessary during our first year of office to pay out over a million and a half dollars for unemployment. Business was not steady; business men were looking about for markets; the purchasing power of the people was lower than it had been for many years. That was the condition that obtained when the government took office. One of the first things we did was to review the estimates that had been placed befo.re council by the officials under the regime of the ministers who had gone out of power, and our first act of retrenchment and economy was that of cutting those estimates down to the extent of over $130,000,000. In doing that we had to exercise great discretion in matters of expenditure. I think the best way to illustrate that is to give to the House the total expenditures for the years preceding- and following the time of the government's accession to office. In 1920, the year in which the armistice was signed, the total expenditure of Canada amounted to $785,869,611. In the year 1920-21, in which the control of expenditure was, with the exception of the last three months, in the hands of my hon. friends opposite, the expenditure amounted to $528,283,199. In 1922 it was $463,652,436, showing a gradual reduction of expenditure. In the year that has just closed a considerable further reduction was effected, so that the total expenditure amounted to $375,213,651.
As well as effecting economies in expenditure it was necessary that we should look also to our revenue. The outlook in the year 1922 was such that if we had carried on affairs as they were left to us by the government that went out of power we would have been face to face with a deficit of $200,000,000 that year.
It was necessary to grapple with that con-
dition, and to that end we had to find more revenue. The revenue in 1920 amounted to $349,000,000, in 1921 to $436,000,000 and in 1922 to $389,898,000. In 1923 the revenue had increased to $405,414,000. We have heard some criticism in the House, and particularly in the country, in public addresses and in representations made through the press, to the effect that the government had increased taxation. Let me say emphatically that it was necessary in some way to provide for the commitments that had been made during the years of the war and after.
If it was necessary for the government to increase taxation, it was necessary only by reason of the fact that the government that-preceded us neglected to make a proper impost of taxation when the people of this country had the money to pay taxation, and I am free to say, and I think the people of the country will agree with me, that any increases in taxation that we found necessary to make were largely along the line of taxation upon those who were in the position to pay. We increased the sales tax, and we have heard a great deal of criticism, especially during the past year, of that increase, but let me say that this was done after the business men and those engaged in industry in this country, those who had experienced the results of the taxation of the former government, and particularly of what is known as the luxury taxes, were ready to say to us, and say without hesitation that the best method of imposing the increased taxation was by means of a sales tax. So I would say to those who criticise that method of raising revenue that it meets with the approval of those who have to pay the revenue very much better than any impost such as the luxury taxes imposed by the former Minister of Finance.
Passing from that phase of the financial situation, we had to provide for a revenue that would not only pay our interest and our running expenses, but also for the whole capital cost of the war. It is not necessary for me to go into detail, because it has been very well put before the House on two or three previous occasions during this session, but I think it is. something that is worth repeating, for if there is one thing more than another that my hon. friends opposite fell down in it was in not providing the necessary revenue to meet the expenditure when money was flowing freely into this country during the war. I say again that it was necessary for us to provide for the capital cost of the war and demobilization, which amounted at the end of the fiscal year 1920 to $1,670,406,242. Aside from that, the previous government added $13,733,333 to the national debt.

The Budget-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)

speechtext:
My hon. friends on the other side are very ready to quote from the United States, but they were not so ready in years past to quote authorities from that country. If my hon. friend will look at the blue books published under the authority of this government and analyse the figures, he will find that those I have presented to the House are correct. There is nothing in the blue books or in any documents published under the authority of the Auditor General of this country that will show anything different. If my hon. friend has to go to foreign countries to bolster up his case and excuse the party he represents for not doing their duty during the war in finding the revenue necessary when such could have been obtained from the people who had the money, he must be in a very bad plight.
I was speaking, when the interruption took place, of the national debt. The national debt at the end of March last was $2,423,367,759.37. In the last two years our debt has increased considerably. In the year 1920-21, which was the first year after the armistice was signed, and a year in which the government of that day should have exercised a careful supervision over expenditure and exerted themselves to the utmost to raise the necessary revenue, the amount of $92,000,000 was added to our national debt. During the fiscal year ending March 31, 1922, $81,000,000 more was added. I may point out that for the last three months of that year this government was liable for expenditure, but the programme for expenditure was largely laid down by our predecessors in office, and all that could be done by us was simply to slow up on the expenditure, and I think it is safe for me to say that if there had not been a strong hand exercised during those three months in controlling expenditure the addition to our national debt would have been much
greater. During the first year we had control of affairs in Canada, our national debt increased by $31,000,000, but last year we are in the happy position of being able to say to the people of this country that our national debt did not increase, but on the contrary showed a net decrease of $30,409,109.37, or an improvement when compared with the year previous of about $61,000,000. That was largely brought about by exercising a strong hand on economy, and also by collecting the taxes that were properly due without fear or favour. If we do not act with firmness and see that those who are able to pay, pay their just share of taxation, we cannot expect to bring Canada back to the era of prosperity which we all so much desire.
It is also to be remembered when considering this phase of the financial situation, that a large part of our expenditure is expenditure which we cannot control. In the year preceding last, our uncontrollable expenditure amounted to over $300,000,000. During the year that has just closed our uncontrollable expenditure has been reduced considerably, and when we analyse the figures closely we find that that reduction in uncontrollable expenditure is largely due to the increased earning powers of our Canadian National Railways. The management of the National Railways has been of such a kind that it has given results in this country; the increase of revenue has been very marked, and the decrease in expenditure in carrying on the railways has been equally, if not even more marked.
One of the principal factors enabling the government to balance the budget this year was the success encountered in the management of the Canadian National Railways, resulting in a reduction of the uncontrollable expenditure this year to about $250,000,000. The balancing of the budget was also made possible by the economies carried out in the general expenditure on ordinary consolidated fund account. These economies were rendered more difficult by the fact that during the war public works in Canada were allowed to stand. I am not criticizing hon. gentlemen opposite because of the fact, I am simply saying that it is the case, and that we encountered that difficulty when we assumed office. We found thes that the public works of the country had deteriorated greatly and in consequence during our first year or two in office it was almost impossible to economize in expenditure of this character. However, although delayed at first in carrying out economy we have striven to make up for lost time, and the estimates presented to the House this session bear evidence as to the
1370	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
sincerity of our efforts along that line. Sir, what do these reductions of expenditure mean to the people of Canada? That has been very clearly demonstrated in the budget brought down last Thursday by the Acting Minister of Finance. The reductions of expenditure made in 1923 amount to $29,000,000, those in 1924 to $59,000,000, and our estimates for the year we are facing, compared with the total estimates for last year, will show a reduction of $46,000,000.
There is one remarkable feature in connection with the reduction of the national debt which deserves special emphasis. It is that there has been a greater reduction of debt than has ever been announced by any previous government. It is a greater reduction than the aggregate reductions which characterized the golden era of Canada's prosperity under the Laurier-Fielding regime, from 1896 to 1911. The reduction made this year is also larger than the aggregate reductions made during the years of Conservative rule from 1911 to 1921. Sir, the budget so recently brought down is one which we may well be proud of, and one that should excite great pleasure among the people of this country.
It is scarcely necessary to refer to the reductions of duty that have gone into effect; they are apparent to everyone. But there is one feature of the tariff question to which I should like to refer. It was argued during the reciprocity election of 1911, and the same argument was brought forward at political meetings during the recess and during the present debate, that the farmers of this country require more protection, that from year to year agricultural products from the United States are being dumped in this country thereby demoralizing the markets of Canada, and that more protection in the matter of grain, vegetable and animal products should be given to our farming population. Sir, from my understanding of the situation no more unreasonable proposition was ever placed before the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite who represent the "interests" of this country-and I do not think it is unfair to them to make that statement -must be extremely anxious to make out a case when they say that the Canadian farmers need more protection. I repudiate any such idea. I say the farmers of the Dominion are not crying out for more protection. Let me devote a few minutes to an analysis of imports of agricultural products that enter Canada, and for the purpose of the comparison I shall take the latest figures available, as given in the trade returns for the nine months from April 1st to 31st Decern-

ber, 1923; it is not possible to get the figures in detail up to 31st March last. The necessity for more protection for the farmer vas set out in the amendment moved to the motion for the adoption of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne this session. Is that claim borne out by the imports of agricultural products entering Canada from the United States? If we look at the trade statement to which I have referred we find the imports of animal and vegetable products-except chemicals, fibres and wood, amounted to $141,493,793. We also imported animal and animal products to the amount of $32,561,941. In analysing Canadian trade we cannot confine it solely to the trade that passes between one country and another. If my hon. friend will look at our total Canadian trade he will see that the balance of trade between Canada and the United States is about $118,000,000 in favour of the United States. That is we still import $118,000,000 more than we sell them, but both the United States and Canada deal with other countries as well as dealing with each other, and if my hon. friend will analyse the trade between Canada and Great Britain he will find that the balance is about equal on the other side of the ledger. So that if we want to have a proper analysis of Canadian trade and our balance of trade, we must take into consideration the trade that goes to all countries. It is unfair to confine it to a comparison of the trade between any two countries. Now, sir, I might say with reference to the balance of- Canadian trade, according to my hon. friend's method of figuring, our exports exceeded our imports by $152,000,000 last year. I think that the management of the Canadian National Railways under the present board are to be commended for the showing they have made. It is not too much to say that I be-
5 p.m. lieve that the government when they secured the services of Sir Henry Thornton as president of the board of management, secured a man who has proven himself to be a real asset to the people of *Canada. His management of the road as illustrated in the returns for the last year has proven that he has given to the country the value he was expected to give, and we believe he will continue to give that value. 
I\e have had a good deal of discussion during the session with respect to branch lines, a discussion touching upon almost every problem presented to the board of management, whose recommendations have been endorsed by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), and submitted to the House for its consideration and decision. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that we all heartily endorse the proposition of the board of management and believe that its adoption will conduce to the betterment of the railway. I desire for a short time to refer to matters that are of more provincial interest and I wish to point out that the province from which I come does not benefit in any way by the extensions which have been proposed and the building of the branch lines. I am raising no objection to that and not making it a ground for objection to the extensions in other provinces. I believe those extensions are all justified, but I may say that while no provision is made, the people in the province of Prince Edward Island have been urging the present government and the previous government to provide for railway extensions and branch lines in that province. The necessity for this is particularly acute, on account of the development that has taken place in the last two or three years in the growing of seed potatoes in the Maritime provinces. This industry has proven to be particularly profitable to our people. They find a very ready market among the people of the southern states, where they do not grow a high grade potato. The seed potato is one of the articles on which we make the American pay the duty imposed by his own government but the production of which we cannot carry on with success any great distance from a shipping point. I think it is safe to say that if a farmer is located four miles, or five miles at the outside, from the shipping point, it is almost impossible to carry on the seed potato business on a large scale, because the transportation costs on such a bulky article are very great. The development of this business has created a desire among our people for short railway extensions. The government in power in 1911 foresaw the position we were in, and provided for a branch line to run from Emerald Junction to New London. The contract was let and signed, and the government which succeeded the government of that day cancelled the contract. The matter stands to-day just as it stood at that time, and those people feel the loss thus sustained by the cancellation of the contract.

sions be made. The present state of affairs is one that cannot obtain indefinitely, as the needs of the people must be met.
I do not wish to detain the House at much greater length. I have referred to many matters that are of interest generally as well as from a local point of view, and in regard to the budget, I think it is one that will appeal to the common people of this country. It makes for a reduction in taxation of $2.70 per capita of our population, or over $13 per family of five. I have now nearly closed all the considerations which I have at present to offer the House on this budget. I have endeavoured to give a distinct and fair view of the financial condition of this country, and of the many obstacles we have encountered in attaining a balanced budget. I have compared the result of our effort with that accomplished by any of our predecessors regardless of the political party in power. I have pointed cut that the budget of this year has not increased the burden of taxation now borne by our people, but that the reductions contemplated will mean a saving of $2.70 to every man, woman and child in Canada, I have referred to the increase in trade and production and have proven beyond the shadow of a doubt that more protection is not essential for the prosperity and success of the Canadian farmer; and I have shown that the injury assumed by the former Minister of Finance to have been perpetrated on our egg and cheese production in Canada is wholly imaginary. Look at the improvement in our railways. To-day they are a real asset to our country; a few years ago they were one of our greatest liabilities. Compare the value of our dollar in the money markets with its quotations in the beginning of 1922. Note the increase in bank deposits and in the volume of our foreign trade. Our production for the year 1923 was over four billions of dollars. The era of prosperity now reached is not the transient effect of an accident, not the short lived success of a day, but the genuine, natural and direct result of the confidence and faith which business and industry have in Liberal policies and principles.
Let us hope that the season of our severe trial is at an end, and that we are at length relieved, not only from the dejection and gloom which a few years since hung over the country, but from the doubt and uncertainty which, even for a considerable time after our prospect had begun to brighten, still mingled with the hopes and expectations of the public.
On our present situation fortunate beyond our more sanguine expectations, let me congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, the House, and my country! And, as I conclude, let me

express my earnest wish, my anxious and fervent prayer, that now in this period of success, for the sake of our present age and of posterity, there may be no intermission in that vigilant attention of parliament to every object connected with the revenue, the expenditure, the resources and the industries, which have carried us through all our difficulties and led to this rapid and wonderful improvement; and that under the favour of Providence we may ensure the continuance of this unexampled progress.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose at this stage of the debate to discuss the tariff issues of the budget. No doubt the House will hear enough on the subject from other members, and should I find it necessary to discuss it later there may be an amendment introduced which will afford me the necessary opportunity. I wish, however, to make one comment upon the budget. I understood the Speech from the Throne foreshadowed the introduction of legislation to reduce taxation on the instruments of production, more particularly on those lines which have their origin in the natural products of the country. This has been carried out in the budget proposals by means of reductions either in the tariff or in the sales tax on the leading lines of instruments of production, such as farming, mining, fishing and lumbering; but it would appear that the paper-making industry has been overlooked, either accidentally or deliberately. It is certainly a business which is based upon the natural produce of the country. It is a very important industry in British Columbia, and there are four papermaking plants in the district I represent alone, as well as similar plants in other parts of the province. It appears to me that it would have been thoroughly in line with the declared policy of the government to have given the very expensive machinery which enters into papermaking-nearly all of which machinery has to be bought in the United States, -a rebate either in the sales tax or in the tariff, for the industry is by no means too prosperous at the present time. If the omission was merely an oversight, I hope the government will see their way to amend it when the resolutions come before the House.
I was sorry not to see either in the Speech from the Throne or in the budget any reference to a treaty with Australia, which was much talked of a year ago. I presume that the government has been unable to negotiate such a treaty at the present time. I hope, however, that it will engage their attention' for the conclusion of a treaty with Australia would be of very material advantage to the progress of British Columbia.

The Budget-Mr. Neill
Now I propose to lay some facts before the House in connection with oriental immigration -not as respects British Columbia alone but all Canada. I know the oriental question is somewhat tiresome to many members, but I do not intend to discuss it in a parochial or even a provincial manner. It is unnecessary to do so, because two years ago the House passed a resolution, placing themselves and the whole of Canada on record as being in favour of effective restriction of all oriental immigration. Therefore it will only be necessary for me to touch on the salient points and keep the discussion, if possible, on the plane of a national question. In fact in view of certain events which are happening to the south of us to-day, I may say it is quite likely to become an international question in the near future. I wish particularly to confine my remarks to an absolutely nonpartisan attitude. In 1922 the House will recall that the British Columbia members and some others debated the oriental question, and that not one of us introduced any note of partisanship; no reflections were cast upon one party or another. The result was that in a comparatively short debate-it lasted only one afternoon and evening-a great deal of what I think was useful information was given to the House, information that had the advantage of being unbiased and of representing the various points of view from which this question is regarded in the West. In sharp contrast to this, I had occasion the other day to look up Hansard for a debate on the same subject in 1913. On that occasion unfortunately a partisan tinge was given to the discussion. It was a very long debate, covering over two hundred pages of Hansard, but its informative value was very much impaired by the fact that every hon. gentleman who spoke took up a violent partisan attitude, and the debate degenerated into a series of reproaches, each party blaming the other for having or not having done something which they should not or should have done.
There are two phases of this question- the Japanese and the Chinese. I shall deal very briefly for the moment with the Chinese phase. When this parliament first assembled in 1922 we had a Chinese Immigration Act, which allowed Chinese to come in practically without limit on payment of a head tax of 8500. After the House two years ago passed the resolution to which I have referred, pronouncing in favour of effective restriction, the government, in the following year, 1923. brought down a Chinese Immigration Bill which allowed entrance of the following classes: Members of the diplomatic service and their servants; Canadian or naturalized Chinamen going away for a visit and coming back to Canada; merchants; students. Under section 9 the minister was allowed at his discretion to permit any particular individual to enter for a strictly limited period, which had to be specified. Section 41 also provided that within ninety days of the act coming into force any Chinaman who was then en route to Canada would be allowed to enter; which of course was a reasonable provision. There was also a section, and a very important one, which required all Chinese to be registered within twelve months, this registration to take place at various designated offices.
It has been said that the act was loosely drawn and provided many loopholes for evasion. There seemed to be too many exempted classes. But results are always the best criterion of the effectiveness of any legislation, so let us see what the results were in this case. I have under my hand the results for seven months after the act came into force. In that time there entered Canada from China 455 Chinese-a large number apparently. But of these 438 came in under section 41-the section allowing Chinamen en route to Canada to complete their journey within 90 days of the passing of the act- and of course this provision will never be available again. So we may dismiss these from our consideration of the effectiveness of the act. This leaves only seventeen to be accounted for. Of these ten were Canadian Chinamen coming back after a visit. Of the remaining seven, five were students, one was a consular servant, and one came in by virtue of section 9, under which the minister could let anyone in at his discretion. It appeared that this man was a student at Berkeley, California, who wished to obtain some data in connection with our universities. As he was coming here not as a student he could not be enrolled as one; therefore he was admitted under section 9, for six months. At the end of five months he went away. So the net result of the operations of the act for seven months is that five Chinese students entered Canada who will have to go away at the termination of their scholastic career, and one consular servant, who also will have to go away when his master dispenses with him.
I think it can be truly said, Mr. Speaker, that in view of this record, this is a really effective measure of restriction, and that it can be regarded as a permanent solution of Chinese immigration-a long fought out question in this country.
There are some 40,000 Chinamen in Canada. Of these only about 6 per cent are women, and consequently the birthrate is very low.

The Budget-Mr. Neill
In fact the birth rate is only 7.6 as compared to 21.4 of white people and 36.8 of Japanese *-note how much more prolific the Japanese are. So the result might well be that the birth rate will hardly keep up with the death rate of those 40,000, and in time we may look to their gradual elimination and the final solution of the Chinese question in Canada. I think British Columbia and Alberta-because Alberta shares in this matter-are to be congratulated, and the members from those provinces are also to be congratulated upon helping, by their non-partisan attitude in this House, to bring about that result, because had we been squabbling and attacking each other no doubt the government would not have felt itself called upon to take any very decisive action. Perhaps we may also congratulate the members of the government who carried out the wishes of the House and of the West in that regard. All this is very satisfactory, Mr. Speaker, but there is no rose without its thorn, there is no ointment without its fly, and there is always a nigger in the woodpile. Before we finish congratulating ourselves on the result of this act we must realize that we are confronted with a very pertinent question from British Columbia and the West generally : Why was this act not made applicable to the Japanese as well? The British Columbia members are well aware, and we emphasized that in the debate two years ago, that the Japanese situation was the more acute, and the resolution was passed not only with the approval of the government but also with an amendment moved by a member of the government largely changing the wording of it, that Canada as a whole stood for the effective restriction not merely of Chinese but of oriental immigration. Nothing could be clearer or more emphatic. And why was it not made applicable to the Japanese? Well, Mr. Speaker, we were told it was because the Japanese objected. I recall an occasion some years ago when I asked the government of the day to close up a certain office. It was a sinecure: there was nothing wrong with the occupant, but he was not doing anything to earn his money and I suggested that in the interests of economy the office should be closed. Of course I got the stereotyped reply that we always get from governments: "We must have a report on this." So in due time a report was made and I was furnished with the information that it would not be possible to close this office, that grave objections existed against such a procedure. Of course I was supposed to be satisfied with that, and I have no doubt it was presumed by the department in question that I would never be heard of again. But with what I have no doubt they
[Mr. Neill.)
regarded as stupid obstinacy, I insisted upon knowing what those grave objections were and who made them, and after the usual delay it turned out that the grave objections were made by the gentleman who occupied the position. That was all the objection; it came entirely from him and it was merely founded on the fact that he did not want to give up the job. We have the same thing here. "Japan objects," but surely, Mr. Speaker, that is not enough: we are entitled to ask and we do ask the Japanese why they object. And what answer do we get? We are met with a plethora of vague and illusory arguments-I will not call them arguments: statements-which cannot stand the test of logic or of the precedent of international law. We hear the argument used, "We are a proud nation"; in fact, I have heard so much about that "proud nation" that it almost gives me nausea. "We are a proud nation," says Japan, "and we cannot tolerate anything that looks like discrimination against our nationals." But is a treaty ever made under which one nation does not give something to another which may be regarded as discrimination against some other nation which is left out of the deal? That is patent; everything of that kind implies directly or indirectly some measure of discrimination. We may be held to be discriminating against the United States manufacturers when we give a very decided preference in our markets to British manufacturers. Why does the United States not call us to account and say:	"This is
a discrimination"-which it certainly is- "against our manufacturers; we demand that you withdraw that legislation." Not long ago we had the instance of the United States putting a very high tariff on cattle and wheat-Canadian cattle and Canadian wheat. The word "Canadian" may not have been inserted in the original tariff, but it was absolutely designed to hit Canadian cattle and Canadian wheat, and I am pretty sure that in the case of the last increase, made a few months ago, by which an even higher duty was imposed on wheat, the words "Canadian wheat" were actually used. And is it not on record that recently there has been talk of their putting an embargo upon these same Canadian products, and Canadian products only? There can be no question at all that the result of that tariff has been the loss of a large market for our western farmers; there is no doubt that it has cost our people millions of dollars. And what have we done about it? We know that it has been bad for us and for our trade. We believe, in fact we hope, as we are entitled to hope, that it has proved harmful also tc

The Budget-Mr. tveill
the United States; and we believe that in time they will realize that a mistake was made both from their point of view and from our point of view, and will repudiate that legislation. But in the meantime what have we done? Did we go down to Washington, rattle the sword in its scabbard, and give them to understand that if such and so was not done, "grave international complications" would ensue-as was done, in fact in connection with the Japanese question in the republic to the south of us a few days ago ? We did nothing of the kind, and had we done so I think we would have been very promptly and very properly told to mind our own business. What we did do was to accept the thing with such resignation as we could muster, recognizing the right of these people to control imports into their country in their own way and to impose what terms they saw fit with regard to such products as should be received. And if that is a proper procedure with regard to products, why not also with regard to people? Why have we not the right to say what people shall come into our country and form the basis of our future citizenship? Even in matters of immigration we find that the United States is discriminating against Great Britain in the establishment of a quota, but we do not find Great Britain, who is so very anxious to get rid of her surplus population, talking threateningly about "grave international complications." Why, Sir, the very policy that we seek to adopt in Canada is followed by Japan herself. Is our policy not this: That we wish to restrict Japanese and oriental immigration generally because we do not want to subject our white population to an intense economic competition with a race whose standards of living are lower than ours? Well, those are almost identically the words which Japan herself uses in restricting the immigration of orientals-orientals, mark you-from China, and also from Korea, the latter a province of Japan. Japan, I say, imposes these restrictions upon the numbers entering her own country, practically in the language I have just quoted, and she does it by Imperial Ordinance No. 352.

speechtext:
I am not in favour of puting a high tariff on food entering Canada at the present moment, but I do not wish to be drawn into a discussion of tariff issues, which I think have no bearing on this subject.
Now I wish to summarize the status of the situation to-day, so that we can see what confronts us with regard to the Japanese. Many years ago the immigration of Japanese into Canada was regulated by our ordinary Immigration Act. We had no special Immigration Act such as we had with respect to the Chinese, but in 1907, owing to the pressure of a large influx of Japanese, the government of the day negotiated what was called a "gentleman's agreement" with the government of Japan. I think the right hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) described it as a somewhat loosely expressed agreement, and I think that is a very good description. There has been a good deal of misconception and a good deal of misunder-
The Budget-Mr. Neill

standing has arisen concerning this mysterious document known as a gentleman's agreement. Once you make something hidden and mysterious all kinds of suspicions and myths and misunderstandings grow up around it. I think it might be profitable to put some portion of that agreement on Hansard, so that we would have something to start from and have a place of ready reference. I might say that a great deal, in fact almost all. so far as I know, that has ever been printed in regard to this gentleman's agreement is found in Hansard in the year 1913. when this debate I refer to was going on. It is not very long and the House will bear with me perhaps if I put it on Hansard, because this is a matter that is going to be of very great importance in the near future, and it is much more convenient to find the agreement in the Hansard of to-day than to turn back ten years ago. Here are the two regulations which form the basis of the gentleman's agreement. The letter is dated December, 1907:
Following is the agreement which was included therein:
The regulations (a) would be sent at once to the governors of the several prefectures of Japan, and the regulations (b) to the consuls of Japan in Canada.
(A)
The following classes of emigrants only are those to whom the Japanese government will grant permission to emigrate to Canada
1.	Emigrants having previously resided in Canada and holding certificates of such residence issued by the Japanese consular authorities in the Dominion, and the wives and children of such emigrants.
2.	Emigrants specially engaged by Japanese residents in Canada for bona fide personal or domestic service, upon production of written evidence of such engagement, attested by the competent Japanese consular authorities.
3.	Contract emigrants, where terms of the contract, works to be done, names and standing of the intended employers are satisfactorily specified; such contracts to be accompanied by a certificate from the Japanese consul of the district where the labourers are to be employed.
In addition to the above, emigrants brought in under contract by Japanese resident agricultural holders in Canada and especially required for the promotion of such agriculture; such contract to be accompanied by the certificate of the Japanese consular authority in the district where the labourers are to be employed.
(B) Copy of Memorandum to Consular Authorities. The consular authorities to whom application is made for the issue of a certificate attesting the genuineness of contracts for the employment of Japanese labour in Canada shall not issue the certificate unless they receive satisfactory evidence that such contract has the approval of the Canadian government.
As an exception to this rule, Japanese consular authorities in Canada may issue certificates to Japanese resident agricultural holders who require Japanese labour for the working of their agricultural lands at the rate of from five to ten labourers per one hundred acres of land held by the applicant.
It does not say whether it is per annum, per day or per month. It continues:

It is necessary, however, that before issuing these certificates all Japanese consular authorities shall exercise great care to ascertain the bona fides of the applicant and will take into close consideration the existing state of the labour market and of public feeling.
With reference to domestic and agricultural labourers mentioned in the regulations, the Japanese government do not contemplate that under existing circumstances these two classes should exceed four hundred annually.
The last sentence I read is not in Hansard; it is in the letter accompanying these regulations, and it follows closely the language used in the correspondence which the right hon. the Prime Minister tabled the other day, so we may conclude that it is fairly correct. It is well known that 400 was the figure referred to. I would like the House to note the language used there:	"The government of
Japan do not contemplate-"; that is the only binding clause in it, the only one that suggests that somebody will do something. "The government of Japan do not contemplate" doing such and so. It is not put any more definitely than that, and it is surely a very vague commitment on which to found what ought to be a treaty.
Now it is easy for me,* and it could very readily be not only easy but cheap for me to stand here and criticise the statesmen of twenty years ago. Times have changed since then, and I do not want to fall into that fault, because conditions were different then from what they are now. But I think two mistakes were made in that connection; first, there was an error made in the principle adopted in making this agreement-the principle by which we should surrender to a foreign nation our right to control our immigration; and the second error was in the details under which it was worked out, inasmuch as they were much too limited. But I must remember, and I will frankly admit, that conditions were different then. Canada was a very young nation in those days, and we did not possess or if we possessed, we had not learned to use the right to make treaties and bargain with foreign nations ourselves. In those days any negotiations of that kind had to be done through the British Embassy in the old country -a very slow, a very long and a very tedious method. Quick action was desirable in this case, and the government of the day and the men who went there to negotiate that agreement probably did the best that could be done at that time. The condition was urgent: the Japanese were coming in at the rate of between seven and eight thousand a year, and we find that after the passing of this agreement, in the following year only 495 came in; so at least it can be well claimed that this agreement, whatever its defects, had an immediate success in that regard. But unfortunately,

The Budget-Mr. Neill
while there was such a violent drop, conditions were such that it did not prevent the numbers rising again, as it did later on. The fact that the agreement was so loosely drawn made it possible to increase, perhaps without infraction of the agreement, the immigration to an extent that we find a few years ago, in 1919, the total immigration from Japan amounted to 1,178-a very big increase indeed.
Now the popular conception of that agreement I think has always been that 400 was the total limit of immigration into Canada.
I know I myself entertained that idea for many years until recently, and I think it was generally accepted in that way; but as a matter of fact far more could come in, as we have shown. In some respects there was almost no limit. We have heard a great deal during the late war of the evils of secret treaties, but these treaties were at least written and in a concrete form; but here is an example of the evils not only of secret treaties but of treaties that were practically unwritten, or at least very loosely expressed in the manner I have indicated. It makes it doubly hazardous to deal with an agreement-an international agreement remember-when it is expressed in this vague way. Now owing to the garbled version we thought that 400 was fixed as the limit of the total emigration; but that restriction of 400 a year was only confined to two classes. One was people employed in domestic service and that does not necessarily mean the employment of females only because the word "personal" was used in the agreement, which might mean men as well as women. The Japanese returns are classified so differently from what they are under our system that it is almost impossible to check the two up and show whether the proper number came in or not. If we were to take the total emigration of Japanese during those sixteen years which the agreement covers we would find that the number clearly had been grossly exceeded. But that would be improper because the return contains a large number of women some of whom were not subject to restriction under the gentleman's agreement. If, on the other hand, we eliminated all the women that would not be fair because a number of them might come in. or perhaps did come in, under the heading of "domestic servants." It is almost impossible to say whether the gentleman s agreement was adhered to or not, but I do find that the following classified people, according to our returns, came into Canada during the sixteen years that agreement was in force: There were 1,139 farmers, 145 mechanics, 484 clerks, 8 miners, and 737 not classified. These are all males. Well, it is apparent that none
of these should have been allowed in, because the gentleman's agreement made no provision at all for the entry of mechanics, clerks, miners or farmers, but only agricultural labourers; and of course in the majority of cases the unclassified might be anything at all. Therefore it is very difficult to say whether the Japanese government adhered to the strict letter of their agreement or not. It may be advisable to concede, for the sake of argument, that they did, because my own argument is based on something different to that.
I have before me a pamphlet issued by the Consul General of Japan in Ottawa in the year 1922. The title of this pamphlet is "Facts about Japanese in Canada and other miscellaneous information." I remember once reading a pamphlet called "Facts and Fancies" and somehow or other the Japanese pamphlet reminds me of it. I see that the title, very properly I think, makes a distinction between "facts about Japanese" and "other miscellaneous information." The suggestion is that the facts are facts and the miscellaneous information may or may not be facts. I think it is a very good definition because there are a great many facts that I do not find in this pamphlet, and a great many of the facts that are stated to be facts are certainly not facts at all. We were all furnished with a copy of this pamphlet at the time of its issue, and it was of course prepared by the Japanese authorities. Now, I turn to page 10 and it gives a statement of Japanese labourers sailing to Canada during the fourteen years between 1908 and 1921, and it shows that the total number of domestic servants that sailed during that period was 1,015. That is according to this little pamphlet. But, Mr. Speaker, it is well known that you can prove anything by figures, especially when you have the preparing of the figures yourself. I have here our census returns which are supposed, at least, to be more or less accurate, and I find that during the same period the emigration from Japan of domestic servants was 110. I am not saying there was deliberate fraud there at all, I do not think so. but when the returns of our government show 110 domestic servants coming to Canada whereas the Japanese returns gives the number as 1,015, the figures in both cases being applicable to the same period it shows how impossible it is to know what number of emigrants is or is not coming in to the country. There is no question but that the same difficulty exists, as regards the emigration of women. Now, the gentleman's agreement said that all women and children could come in provided the women were wives of Japanese in Canada; and, of
The Budget-Mr. Neill

course, any one would say the agreement meant the wives of Japanese then in Canada. However, I think there can be no question, although it is very difficult to prove-there is no question I think after careful consideration of these statistics-that there was a good deal of evasion practised in that regard. Many of these men, the majority of them, must have been single when they came, and the evasion I am afraid was worked in this way: The Japanese women could come in if they were the wives of Japanese in Canada. Well, what happened? Somebody in Japan, issued a book called The Picture Bride's Book the same as one of Eaton's catalogues, and the Japanese living in British Columbia would turn the pictures over and when he came to a picture that he liked he would select it and forward it with a sum of money to Japan. On the return trip the woman would come accompanied by a guarantee that she was the party represented. She brought with her a certificate of some form or proof that she was the wife of this man. I have no doubt that when she arrived the man married her willingly enough provided there was a certain amount of resemblance between the woman herself and the picture he had paid for. That is how, I think, the thing was worked. I do not say it was done with the connivance or knowledge of the Japanese government, but it was certainly done by the nationals of Japan. The same thing happened, although upon a larger scale, in California. There it was carried out on such a wholesale scale, it developed into such a scandal and caused such a fuss, that in deference to the pressure of public opinion the Japanese government themselves interfered and stopped the practice. For the Picture Bride's Book they substituted the " Kandokan " system, but I believe a great many more Japanese were brought in under the latter than under the former. I think there is no doubt that a great many of these women who came to Canada as wives were not wives. If we turn to page 13 of the pamphlet I have already referred to we find a statement of Japanese passengers returned from Canada. On page 9 is given another statement showing the number of Japanese passengers that sailed to Canada. Now if we deduct the one from the other it shows that in fourteen years, taking in the period from 1908 to 1921, there were 113 more Japs went back to Japan than came to this country and naturally the inference is " What on earth are the British Columbia people kicking about, if as a result of sixteen years' operation of the gentleman's agreement there were 113 fewer Japs in Canada than there were at the beginning." Now those are Japanese statistics. 
Let us turn now to our own statistics, and I think our census returns can be held to be more or less reliable. Our census returns show that in 1911, which was three years after the beginning of this period remember, there were in Canada 9,021 Japs. Now if we wish to get the correct number for 1908 we must make a deduction from the figures of 1911 to allow for emigration in those three years. A reasonable proportion, perhaps, would be 7,000, but to be well within the mark I shall say 7,500. In 1921 according to our census returns the number was 15,868 so that at the end of fourteen years the increase was at least 100 per cent. I will also refer to page 13 of this pamphlet, where they quote the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the debate in May, 1922, and he in turn quotes a remark made in April 1919 by the Hon. Mr. Calder then in the government, wherein he uses the following language:
I have gone into the situation very carefully, and I can tell the House that the agreement has been lived up to by the Japanese government to the letter. As a matter of fact, taking the figures for the last four or five years there are in the neighbourhood of four or five hundred fewer Japs in Canada to-day than there were in 1914.
This assertion is in line with the one I quoted from the pamphlet and yet I have quoted our own census returns, which show an increase in the Japanese population of 100 per cent.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
