subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
When the House adjourned
at six o'clock I had been pointing out the discrepancy between a statement quoted in the House by Mr. Calder, Which no doubt was made in perfect good faith, as well as a statement in a pamphlet got up by the Japanese

The Budget-Mr. Neill
Consul, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, the records as disclosed by our Canadian census. The same thing can be observed in the United States; and it is remarkable how closely the conditions there approximate, either in the past or now, with the conditions in this country. Under pressure of public sentiment some years ago the United States government proposed to introduce an oriental exclusion law, but by reason of strong representations on the part of the Japanese they confined themselves instead to the introduction of a Chinese exclusion law, entering into a gentleman's agreement with the Japanese, which was very similar to our gentleman's agreement with those people. Under the Chinese exclusion law, in a given period of years thereafter, the Chinese population in California, which was a very large one, decreased by 50 per cent. I might point out that this gentleman's agreement with the Japanese was intended, as it was actually stated, to take the place and serve the same purpose as an exclusion act; but to save the face of the Japanese nation it was agreed that the arrangement should take that form. There was no four hundred limit as in our case; it was supposed to be absolute. Yet in the same period as I have indicated in which the Chinese population decreased by 50 per cent, the Japanese population increased by 25,000. That I think speaks for itself. This gentleman's agreement, both in the United States and in Canada, has proved itself a failure. I am willing for the sake of argument, if that will save time or save the face of the Japanese government, to admit that I at least for the moment am unable to prove that that government has been knowingly privy to any fraud in the carrying out of this agreement. The returns are so involved and divergent in their purport that it is impossible to prove anything of the kind, and I say frankly that I could not to-day show that the Japanese government were privy to any fraud in carrying out the terms of the agreement. But that statement does not apply to the nationals of Japan, who were acting more or less on their own authority. I am not looking at the methods but at the results; and the net result of this gentleman's agreement, which was intended to restrict, has not been to restrict but instead to increase the Japanese population, in a given period, 100 per cent. It has resulted in a large increase, out of all proportion, in the number of Japanese women coming into the country; and with their large birth rate of 31.8 per cent, nearly 40 per cent greater than that of Canada as a whole, the result will be by natural means to largely in
crease the Japanese population in this country and thereby foment and increase the economic disturbance which the presence of these people creates in whatever part of Canada they are living. Therefore I maintain that the agreement has proved a failure in that it * has not restricted Japanese immigration. So much for that.
In 1910 the Immigration Act was amended, and section 38, we find, gave the minister power to prohibit for a stated period, or permanently, the landing in Canada of immigrants belonging to any race deemed unsuited to the climate or the requirements of Canada, or of any immigrants of any specified class, occupation or character. That certainly gave us power to exclude Japanese or any similar class of immigration. But we do not have it now because in 1919 that section was repealed and a much stronger section put in its place, section 13, which not only goes the distance I have already recited but includes power to the minister to reject immigrants who, in his opinion, are undesirable from their probable inability to become readily assimilated. That is all on that subject, which I merely introduce now that I may refer to it in my general argument later on.
In 1913 we passed an act adopting a treaty of trade and commerce which had been entered into between Great Britain and Japan. It was devoted entirely to trade and shipping matters, but it contained a clause which allowed the nationals of either race to live and trade in the country of the other contracting party. Now, the act by which we ratified that treaty contained a provision which said that nothing in the treaty itself, or in our act, should be held to repeal or affect the provisions of our immigration law. There was a very long and acrimonious debate over the matter and on some correspondence which had passed between the government of the day and the Japanese authorities. The discussion centered for a long time around the point: Did this correspondence in any way modify or qualify the clause which stipulated that the treaty would be subject to our immigration law? The leader of the government of the day, Sir Robert Borden, said emphatically and repeatedly-and he was backed up by his ministers-that in his opinion the correspondence did not affect the stipulation, and never was intended to affect it, but was purely of an academic character, and that the section still stood good in law and in practice making the treaty subject to the Immigration Act of that day at least.
There was further discussion as to the point: Would this treaty be subject to any future amendment of our immigration law.
13S8

The Budget-Mr. Neill
There was no doubt that it was subject to the Immigration Act of that day. There was a long discussion on this point also, which developed some divergence of opinion, but I notice that the right hon. gentleman who is now the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) made a strong argument to the effect that the act of that date gave power to the minister to make regulations, and that this power could not be affected or vitiated in any way, but would always endure, and that under it we could make any further restrictive regulations that we might deem advisable. He made a strong and, I think, forcible argument in that regard. In any case, whether that is so or not, there is no question that the act of that day at least applied to the treaty then made. I would remind hon. members that this act contains section 38 which I have quoted.
Now, to summarize the situation up to date. We have, first, this loosely drawn agreement which, if adhered to by the Japanese government, was at least evaded by their nationals, especially in regard to the immigration of their women, resulting in a 100 per cent increase of the Japanese population. Then we have this treaty, subject, however, to section 38 of our Immigration Act, and perhaps subject also to section 13 of the 1919 act, which was even more stringent. Then we have the agreement made by the right hon. leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) and recorded in the correspondence which he brought down a few weeks ago, whereby the number of Japanese immigrants under the gentleman's agreement was reduced from 400 to 150, but leaving intact all the other provisions of the original agreement. Then finally we have the resolution-and I think it is a very important one-passed by this House two years ago-in May 1922-affirming the opinion that we should have effective restriction of all oriental immigration. I leave myself in the hands of the House, Mr. Speaker, to say whether the foregoing is not a fair summary of the situation as it exists to date.
Beyond that we have two other phases that have only recently arisen. We have the fact that in California the legislature some time ago passed legislation forbidding Japanese to own, lease or hold agricultural land. That act was sustained by the Supreme Court of the United States. It practically means that something like 50,000 Japanese have been thrown out of occupation in California and the adjoining states. It naturally follows that there will be more or less of a desire on the part of at least a proportion of those 50,000 Japanese to make their way into Canada' by legitimate or illegitimate means. I saw in the 
paper the other night that about 20,000 of them may go to Mexico. I hope so.
Ihe other phase is the outcome of the Immigration Act wdiich the American congress recently passed, one of the most important features of which is the practical exclusion of Japanese immigration. This is the first time they have taken such a drastic course, and apparently they have gone at it in a very whole-hearted way. I have had some correspondence with the honourable congressman who had charge of that particular measure. He writes me that they had there the same difficulty that we have had, the difficulty of convincing congressmen from the eastern part of the States that the Japanese problem was not confined to the Pacific coast; but apparently they have at last managed to convince congress that the situation involved the whole country. Congress passed the measure by a large majority, some 330 for and some 72 against. The Washington papers of last week stated that the act was coming before the Senate and it was anticipated that the restrictive clause would be struck out, but that there was some feeling in favour of such a restriction and there might possibly be a close vote. That was the expectation a few days ago. But what happened, Mr. Speaker? We see in the papers to-day that the measure passed the Senate by a very large majority, 72 senators being in favour of retaining the clause and only 2 voting for its deletion.
Now, we have an Asiatic Germany as well as a European Germany. Just at the very moment when diplomacy was specially called for we find the true tactics of the Germans in evidence-the Japanese came down with a boast and a threat: the old game of the sword and the drum. At the psychological moment the Japanese ambassador practically threatened the United States as to what would happen if the legislation was passed. I think probably nothing tended more to its passing the Senate than this teutonic attitude. For instance, one senator said that:
The right and power of congress to exclude " whom it will " was not to be challenged. Other nations were aware of that, and it was unnecessary to seek the consent of any nation to proceed.
Another senator said:
The protest of the Japanese ambassador against the exclusion provisions was an impertinent communication, which would not be tolerated even by a fourth-rate power.
I presume that the measure will be ratified by the President and become law. I have not for years heard any news of a political character which has given me more satisfaction than this action by congress. As to this I feel like saying with the prophet, "Now

The Budget-Mr. Neill
is our salvation nearer than we believed." Certainly it is nearer than when I saw this correspondence brought down a few weeks ago. The very fact that that legislation is passed will also tend to set the tide of Japanese immigration still stronger towards our shores, and it behooves us to be especially careful in guarding our rights in this respect. For that reason I was sadly disappointed when I saw the correspondence and saw what arrangement had been made with the Japanese authorities. I was disappointed in two ways. First, in the immediate results: True there has been a considerable reduction, but the door is still left open, especially to women, and that in many ways is very undesirable.
I have looked up the immigration returns since then, and I find that there has been a substantial reduction. Fewer Japanese have come in since that agreement was arrived at than before, but unfortunately there is nothing to prevent an increase of the numbers later. This condition always arises when we make an agreement of that character with Japan. The last time it dropped from 7.000 to 495, and afterwards it went up to 1,200. Here it has dropped considerably, but the possibility is there, the opportunity is there, and we have no guarantee that it will not in the future, as in the past, go up again to a very large extent. We may have next year 1.178 instead of the number that it is now, or even more. Now, had the exemption been fixed, not at 150 of certain grades or classes or occupations, but at 150 of all grades of Japanese, the situation would have been much more satisfactory. It could not even then be regarded as a permanent solution, for nothing short of definite and permanent exclusion would reach that end, but it might be regarded as a temporary solution because the power would then be vested in us to check this immigration as it came in. So it *would have been taking a proper step to confine it absolutely to 150; it would have been a simple matter of counting heads- which, by the way, Mr. Speaker, is the onty safe way in dealing with a question of this kind in connection with orientals.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he was Minister of Marine and Fisheries helped us a great deal out on the coast by introducing regulations in his department reducing the number of Japanese who could get, fishing licenses. We appreciated his action, and it will be remembered by many fishermen on the Pacific long after some of his more notable achievements have been forgotten. A few' months ago it became 89
necessary, in continuance of this reduction policy, to refuse to renew certain Japanese licenses, and the question that naturally arose was, whose licenses should be refused? An extraordinary situation at once developed. There had been no question of suspicion in regard to the men who had the licenses the previous year; there was no suggestion that there had been anything improper about their naturalization papers or their licenses. But this year as soon as it was discovered that some of these men had to forfeit their licenses, affidavits commenced to come in to the effect that certain fishermen w'ere holding their licenses improperly. These representations were to the effect, for instance, that a certain man in whose name a license had been issued had been dead for two years. Or, they would say, "This man over here was never on the west coast at all; he was up at the Skeena; this other man is in Japan," and so on. The unfortunate official who had to decide this question found his desk stacked up with affidavits, each one more vehement and positive than the last one, alleging that absolute fraud had been perpetrated by certain numbers of these Japanese, the whole idea, of course, being that if they could get these men whom they were accusing eliminated, they would themselves be able to get licenses. The official, of course, gave the accused persons an opportunity of rebutting the charges made, and presently an equal number of equally vehement affidavits were filed in defence of those accused and charging every crime in the calendar against those wTho had originally made the complaints. Now, it is of no importance to my argument which of these affidavits were wrong, which of the bunch perjured themselves or whether they all did. As to that I do not know, but it was a revelation of how little we know of what goes on when we are dealing wfith orientals. Had it not been for that chance occurrence in connection with the elimination of some of these men we would never have heard any suggestion that there had been any impropriety about the way they were holding their licenses. It therefore makes me anxious to see that the immigration, if it must be under the gentleman's agreement, is confined to a very definite number that would take in all classes, so that it would only be a question, as I have said, of counting heads.
So much for the result, so to speak, of that agreement; now7 a word as to the method. I was very sorry indeed to see the gentleman's agreement maintained. I had

The Budget-Mr. Neill

hoped it would have been withdrawn. It was an opportunity to place Canada, I was going to say, almost on a pedestal, certainly to bring her into considerable prominence in the North American continent, probably among all civilized nations, as having been the first, though a small and a young nation, to take a firm stand in the matter, to tell the Japanese that we were done with gentlemen's agreements and that hereafter we were going to be mistress in our own house. We should have been in the enviable position of having given a lead in the matter and the great republic to the south would have had no recourse but meekly to follow our example. Unfortunately we lost that opportunity. Now, this government since it has been in office-and I am not complaining of it in any way at all-have emphasized, I will not say the independence of Canada, because that does not express what I mean and might be misunderstood, but, if I may use the word in connection with a nation, they have emphasized the individuality or the individual entity of Canada as a nation. We saw that in the determination to negotiate our own halibut treaty with the United States, and also to sign it ourselves. We saw it more recently in the correspondence in connection with the Lausanne treaty, and in some other matters that I do not recall at the moment. But it is ten times more necessary that we should take such a stand in connection with immigration and ten times more necessary that we should control it ourselves than it was in any of the instances I have mentioned, and I regret very much that the same policy was not adopted. We should have told the Japanese nation that their objection to our restricting their immigration on the ground of economic competition was not a tenable one, in view of the fact that they themselves adopted exactly the same procedure in restricting immigration into Japan of Chinese and of their own subjects from Korea. We should have told them that we could no longer hand over to somebody else the control of one of our fundamental rights. We should have told them that entrance into Canada is not a right to be possessed by anyone, but is entirely a privilege to be retained by us and controlled entirely by us in our own interest. With the exception of this particular instance in connection with ourselves and the States there is no record in history of one nation, except under stress of military force and subjection, giving up such an important right to another nation. As I say, the two instances I gave were exceptions, and we find that the United States has now re-

pudiated the arrangement. I hope that it is our intention to follow suit. We should have told the Japanese nation that the gentleman's agreement was a generation old, that while we were then a young nation, what was suitable then is not suitable now. We have grown up and we must forget those boy and girl entanglements of the past. We are now a man among men, a nation among nations. We have the full rights of a nation, but we shall never be accorded recognition of those rights in the civilized world if we do not exercise and maintain them to the full. Surely, Mr. Speaker, we have as much right as Australia or New Zealand to set up as our ideal of citizenship, a white Canadian manhood. It is so in Australia, it is practically so in New Zealand; why should it not be so here?
I do not suggest for a moment that this matter should have been put up to the Japanese nation aggressively, or in any way offensively at all. It should have been put up resolutely and firmly, and with this fixed determination, to get it into the minds of the Japanese statesmen that this matter had got to be settled, and that there was only one way to settle it, that the best solution both for them and for us was an effective measure of restriction. I say for both of us advisedly. For us because we will never be satisfied with anything less, and the longer it is left the more difficult it will be, with Canadian-born Japanese children growing up in increasing numbers to deal adequately with the situation; and it will be best for the Japanese nation too to understand once and for all, and understand now. what I do not believe they have grasped, that they must not think they can look here for an outlet for their overflowing population. It will give them an opportunity to turn to some other country where perhaps they will even be welcomed. They no doubt have the idea, and there is much in our past history to justify it, that perhaps in time they would overcome our prejudice against them and that we would allow them to over-run our country. The sooner they understand that is not so, and that our determination is for all time, the better for them, because it will afford them an opportunity to turn to other spheres and possibly to nations where they really would be welcomed.
The records of political history, and our own experience as business men, both unite to tell us that no arrangement can be satisfactory when it is framed in such vague and indeterminate language as this so-called, gentleman's agreement. "It is not contemplated"-that is the operative clause, so to speak, the binding portion of this agreement.

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin
"It is not contemplated"-that is all. I wonder how hon. gentlemen would like to see an expression like that on a note given by some creditor of theirs-"It is not contemplated." That is the only binding clause in the agreement. The whole thing is wrapped up-we surround it ourselves inevitably, it is not in the thing itself-with pretence and suspicion, because pretence leads to suspicion. On the one hand, we are in the position of saying, "Gentlemen, this is an agreement, but it is not binding." On the other hand, we say, "Gentlemen, this is binding, but it is not an agreement." Which is right? They both cannot be, and yet we alternately use both, that is the situation.
I would certainly ask the government not to regard as final, indeed, there was nothing to suggest that they were final, the negotiations that are revealed in the correspondence brought down a few weeks ago. I would not ask them to renew those negotiations, but rather to drop them, and to come before this House with a bill constituting a true measure of effective restriction, which indeed would be thoroughly in accord with the expressed wish of this House as recorded in the vote of May, 1922, when we passed unanimously a resolution that we were in favour of effective restriction of all oriental immigration. I would appeal, I would pray the Prime Minister-I would paraphrase Scripture and ask him to forget the things which are behind and press towards the mark for the prize of our high calling. In this case the prize, the grand prize, would be the realization of our ambition to create in Canada a white Canadian citizenship, a citizenship all white, and all Canadian.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to express the regret that we all feel on this side of the House at the enforced absence through illness of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). We hope he may soon recover; we believe it is the hope of the country at this particular time that he may have a speedy recovery. I think the country feels that it is a misfortune that he should have been taken ill at the present time.
I wish to say a word in respect to some of the statements .made by the minister, without portfolio (Mr. Sinclair) who spoke before six o'clock. Briefly I will take his own figures. He tells us that we are importing into this country from the United States $82,000,000 worth of products of the farm, which are entering into direct competition with our own farm products. According to him we must not increase our tariff; we must not defend ourselves against the nation that practically puts an embargo on our products; we are to 891
crawl-and he makes the excuse that we must not do it because of the artisans of this country. Well, all I can say to the hon. gentleman is that he and this government are not worrying very much about the artisan just now. I come from a section of the country that is right up against that competition, a section close to the border, and I am not afraid to tell him that we want a tariff and an increased tariff on that kind of product.
He says that it is impossible to put a tariff on vegetable products because of the artisans; it is impossible to put a tariff on early fruits because of the artisans. Let me tell him that the United States are several weeks in advance of us in our section of the country; their products come in several weeks earlier, and I would ask the minister or any other member of the government if those early fruits from the United States that spoil the early market of the growers in the province of Ontario and all along the border are for the artisans of this country. The people that use that stuff, selling at high prices, are the people that can well afford to pay, and it is from those people the tax should be taken, and not from the artisans. Who of the artisans in Ontario are buying tomatoes at 40 cents a pound, for they are coming in right at the present time. Are the artisans of this country likely to buy these tomatoes from t'he full pay roll that is going to come from this so-called reduced taxation, these reduced duties that are coming into force?
Take eggs, which the minister (Mr. Sinclair) spoke of. The same thing applies there. Fowls mature a month earlier in the warmer climate of the United States than they dc with us. We have to house our cattle and our poultry over a longer period. Why should the extra profit in that business be handed over to the United States people? Is it not pretty nearly time something was done for that particular industry?
Now I want to say a word to the minister without portfolio in reference to this so-called surplus and this so-called saving. The minister and the government put me in mind of a merchant who used to meet his bills by means of a note. When he had signed the note he would shove the bill in the drawer and say, "Thank God, that is paid." Now, that is exactly what occurred in this railway situation; it was exactly the same thing over again. We have bills payable coming due that this government will have to meet. Why should it not put those in its bills payable ledger? I very well remember that last year the Minister of Finance, who is unfor-
The Budget-Mr. Chaplin

tunately ill at the present time, in delivering the budget said, not exactly in these words but to this effect: "Dear me, up to the time that I met that unfortunate railway deficit I had a surplus. But I met that unfortunate deficit. It knocked my surplus out but I paid it." Now, this government has not met the obligation-it passes by on the other side and forgets to meet it. It has not been as frank as the Finance Minister was last year. The government thinks it is going to get the people of this country to believe that it has a surplus when in reality it has a liability on its hands. The government really ought to be frank about the matter but that is what it is not. It looks to me as if there was a sort of arrangement under which every minister comes along with a prepared statement of a campaign character, a statement got up in first class style. These ministerial statements are being issued to us in reams. It is against the rule to read speeches in this chamber but the Minister of Finance and young members of the House are allowed the privilege as a courtesy. And so we are getting these ministerial statements. We have had a number, I wonder if there are any more to come.
Before entering into any further criticism of the budget resolutions I wish to lay before the House an analysis of the French treaty.

In the first place, however, I desire to say that I am not opposed to a treaty with France or with any nation. A minister of the Crown gets up this afternoon and gives us a long tirade about the tremendous struggle the members of the cabinet have had to stop each other from spending, and to stop the deputy ministers from spending for them, because of the economy they wanted to practise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have shown you the loss in revenue on the articles coming into Canada. I desire to give the other side of the story also and to show exactly
9 p.m. what we have had out of the treaty. Unless I tell the whole story I might be accused of keeping' something back.

What was the
estimate as to the loss?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance last year estimated the loss at between $500,000 and $800,000. My calculations are based upon the ten-month period ending at the close of January, 1924, and the calculations in regard to the French treaty are of the same dates. The exports of Canada to France for these ten months were, in round figures, $15,400,000 while our importations from that country amounted to $13,100,000, leaving a balance in our favour of $2,300,000 for that period. The principal items that comprised that $15,000,000 were wheat, sugar,
pulp, including sulphite and mechanical pulp, agricultural implements, lobsters, salmon, pig lead, ore, asbestos, coal, tar and rubber goods. There are a number of smaller items which I shall not weary the House by detailing; I am not omitting them for any other reason than that I do not wish to delay the House. These however are the most important items. During this period that I have stated France took from us, in wheat, $6,400,000, in sugar $1,600,000; pulp, sulphite and mechanical, $1,467,000; pig lead, $266,000; ore, $115,000; asbestos, $378,000; coal, $50,000; tar, $350,000; agricultural implements, $1,600,000; rubber goods, $400,000; lobsters, $400,000; and canned salmon, $1,200,000. This makes a total of something over $14,000,000 out of the $15,000,000, leaving out odds and ends in other items which are too small to mention. In respect to wheat and sugar no change was made in the French treaty and we obtained no advantage in wheat. We had last year under the treaty the same advantage that we enjoyed before; and the same is true of sugar, of pulp, of lobsters, of pig lead, of ore, asbestos, coal and tar. There were only two items in the list in regard to which we derived any advantage, these being agricultural implements and rubber goods. I must say that we got a real advantage in agricultural implements, and at the time I noticed this I said that some of our manufacturers would benefit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: What was the increase in agricultural implements over the year before?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
There was an increase of $800,000. Let us take the item of salmon. It will be remembered that when I criticised the treaty last year my complaint in regard to canned salmon was that although we were selling them a good deal of salmon the gentlemen who had made the treaty came back with an increased duty on this commodity, and I asked the question w'hether it was feared that we were selling too much fish to France. The result, at any rate, was a loss in salmon and lobster equal to the gain which we derived in agricultural implements. In other words, we lost on salmon and lobster $800,000. It will be observed that these various items that I have indicated, such as wheat, sugar, pulp, pig lead, ore, asbestos, coal and tar, are all purely raw materials; and my complaint against the French treaty was that quite evidently France did not want to buy from us any manufactured products or any article that had any finish on it. They bought, as I have stated $6,400,006 worth of wheat. But
The Budget-Mr. Chaplin

Germany takes $6,000,000 worth of flour; and Germany to that extent is a better customer. Now, I am not making any apology for Germany, but I am ready to trade with everybody on an absolutely fair basis. And that is the remark I made in regard to the United States a few minutes ago: let us trade on a fair basis which will give us a show. Last year we shipped to France, of wheat, 5,665,000 bushels; to Belgium, 9,232,000 bushels; to Italy, 13.451,000 bushels.
The Minister of Finance the other day took a good deal of pains to inform us that Canada had a favourable trade balance. We are all glad to know that#and it is a good thing that we should have such a balance. Indeed, one of our troubles is that we have been buying too much; and if we bought a little less it would, I think, be better for some of us. Let me point out to the minister that-leaving Britain and the United States out of consideration for the moment-Italy shows the best trade balance with us of any of the Furopean nations. The favourable trade balance with her is $16,000,000; Japan, among the smaller nations, comes next with $14,000.000; Belgium, $9,000,000; Germany, $7,000,000; the Netherlands, $3,600,000 and France $2,300,000. I am not blaming France for this; I am blaming our ministers. It is with the government, that the responsibility rests. France made a good treaty; we did not; and that is the whole matter. There is no use in trying to evade that fact, because it cannot be denied; and our arrangement with them is not going to work in any other way than to our disadvantage. I took the trouble to criticise the treaty last year, running the risk of being wrong; but the truth of what I said at that time has been demonstrated. Let me give further particulars as to how the treaty has worked out. To begin with, the treaty gives to France the right to have a fixed duty on a considerable list of goods; and if we wanted to change the tariff to-morrow we could not do so, so far as these articles are concerned. The queer thing about it is that some of the very goods on which they have a fixed duty are covered by the treaty. But do you suppose, Mr. Speaker, that the rates of duty on French goods entering France are the same as our rates of . duty on French goods entering Canada? Naturally one would think that in such a treaty the rates of duty would be the same; but they are not. Take, for instance, canned vegetables. When the treaty was made-of course, I must offer this explantation because the franc has changed somewhat in value in the interval-canned vegetables could enter Canada at a cent a pound,

and our exports to France were subject to a duty of S1./0 per hundred pounds, or If cents a pound. Again, automobiles and similar articles come in here at a duty of 25 per cent, but when we send them to France they are subject to a duty of 35 per cent. And this is called a treaty!
Now, let me trace the history of the canned vegetable trade to show how the trade has worked out under this treaty. My calculations are based for the ten months ending January in each year. In 1923 we sold to France 1,394,000 pounds of canned vegetables, and in 1924 only 21,000 pounds; during the same period last year they sold us 381,000 pounds. Before the treaty was made the French duty was 47 francs per 100 kilogrammes; by the treaty this was raised to 54 francs. I figure the franc at the date of the treaty to have been worth about 6f cents. The duty on our canned vegetables going into France is If cents a pound, while on the French commodity entering Canada our duty is a cent a pound. That is how the treaty lias worked out on this commodity. Then take canned fruits. They sold us 16,000 pounds in 1923, and in 1924 they had increased that quantity to 165,000 pounds, while we sold them nothing. In fact their minimum tariff duty was too high for us to do business on. Then take condensed milk. For the ten months to January 1922, we sold France $568,000 of canned milk, and early in the spring of 1923, before the treaty came into force, we sold them $118,000 more. Since the treaty has been in effect,-five months,-we have sold them only $1,325 worth. The duty on condensed milk was raised 50 per cent. At the time I asked the minister whether they wanted to stop us from doing business with France. Now hon. members see the result. Take the case of butter. The Minister of Justice is not in his seat to-night, and I cannot blame him for the way our trade has been affected by this treaty, but he had something to say last session about butter. He told the House that the idea was to sell fresh butter to France. I was glad to get the information. He also informed the House that;
The Quebec government had made a contract with a firm in Belgium for 20,000 boxes of butter at 60 pounds to the box. The hon. gentleman can figure how much that amounts to.
Well, I have figured that it amounts to a very considerable quantity-1,200,000 pounds. Of course, I was very glad to get the information. But on looking up the trade returns to date I am surprised to find that during the ten months we shipped to Belgium only 266,000 pounds of butter. I wonder where the other million pounds have melted. Per-

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin
haps the contract referred to may have been merely an option, or an agreement of sale. However, I cannot blame the minister for that. He said he did the best he could and wanted to sell our butter to France. The truth is that we have not sold France one single pound of butter. As to cattle, our sales have decreased about two-thirds. We sold to France some oatmeal before the treaty came into effect; that trade is gone. We sold her some oats; that business is gone. We sold her some clover seed; that business has decreased. We sold her some hay; that business has decreased also. We sold her some canned lobster, to which I have already referred; that trade is cut in half, from $708,000 to $402,000. Our exports of agricultural implements to France have increased by $800,000. But our export of canned salmon has decreased $500,000. Our export business in auto parts has decreased somewhat, but the loss is not worth troubling about.
It will be remembered that when this treaty was before the House for ratification we found it contained a long list of about two hundred chemical products, the names of which no one knew the meaning of, but a few of these were picked out as being especially interesting to Canadian shippers. They are as follows: sulphate of ammonia, crude, calcium carbide, formic aldehyde, tri-oximethylene, acetone, acetic acid, acetate of sodium. The gentlemen who got this list up evidently were ashamed of the long list of 200 articles, so they kept it out of the book of particulars and just left these few in. I have looked carefully over the list and I cannot find one of the articles in the index of trade returns, which shows that so far as we know there have been no exports. Of these ten items that are important to Canadian trade, not one dollar's worth goes out to France.
For the benefit of some hon. members who have probably never seen a copy of the American tariff I would like to read a few words that appear on the front page of the 1922 tariff, as showing what some people who make tariffs somewhere have in their minds. I quote:
To provide revenue, to regulate commerce with foreign countries, to encourage the industries of the United States, and for other purposes.
We can all have our own ideas as to what the "other purposes" are. We have met those other purposes here; we see them in the placing by the United States of a rate of 42 cents on wheat, a rate of 8 cents a dozen on eggs against our 3, a rate of 8 cents a pound on butter against our 3-and we have not the
nerve, or have not a government with the nerve, to meet them.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) gave us yesterday a very glowing picture of the wonderful strides that Canada made during that halcyon period between 1896 and 1911. He was so much interested, however, in his well prepared speech that he did not want to have anybody interrupt him to ask a question. I tried to get his attention, but no, he would not listen to anybody. I hope we shall not have any more of these prepared speeches, because you cannot get a chance to say a word to a man. However, we had a very fine speech-a well written speech. The hon. gentleman described in a pitiful way the state of this country from 1878, when that terrible Tory government came into power and put the National Policy into effect. Well, I can tell that minister that I passed through that period. I was in Ontario all the time and I can tell him-and I defy any person in the House or out of it to deny it-that this country in its whole history never passed through a rvorse period than the years immediately prior to 1878. I have no quarrel with what he says about the period between 1896 and 1911-not at all. I may differ from him, however, as to the reason why the conditions were better then. If the Liberal party in those days had carried out their pledges they would not be able norv to talk about that as a halcyon period. I would like to have asked the minister-I do not see him yet-what he considered a- high protectionist policy. I would like to know what he thinks a high protectionist tariff is. I would like to ask any of the ministers what they consider a high tariff-25 per cent? 30 per cent, or something of that kind? I would not, however, expect any of them to answer. The Minister of the Interior forgot that the high protectionist party was in power at the time. We have a book of trade returns published by the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) and on pages 10 and 11 a list is given of import and export returns with respect to articles that are free and also, shown separately, to articles that bear duties. This table indicates to a hair's breadth what tariff was collected on the articles subject to duty, and the information goes back to 1868. And what do we find? That the period betw'een 1896 and 1911 was characterized by the highest average tariff for a period of that length in the whole history of Canada. Now I am not quarrelling with that, I approve of it; I am not finding any fault. But when a minister gets up and says, "Why, we put into effect a tariff policy that built up this

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin
country," I want to let him know what they were doing at that time; he must have been asleep. This country was built up on a policy that the Liberals grabbed when they came into power and that they hung on to until they went out, and they went out of power because they insisted on bringing in reciprocity. That is what put them out of the game.
The Minister of the Interior further said, "Why, we are making a tariff for five and a half million people; we are making a tariff for the bulk of the people of this country; we are reducing the tariff so that these people can be relieved of their burden," Well, what is the relief afforded? It is on an article like agricultural implements, where the reduction is from 10 to 6 per cent. If the proposal is really an honest one, why do the government not reduce the duty on an article that the whole nine million people of our country consume? If they want to reach out and do the greatest good to the greatest number, why do they not reduce the duty on boots and shoes which we all wear?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I do not want anybody
to misunderstand me-I am simply asking the question. I am not in favour of that; not at all, and I would not vote for it. But if my hon. friends opposite are sincere in what they are doing they will put it into effect, and so will the gentlemen to my left who are supporting this government. To them I say, no longer are you the dilapidated annex; you are the overflow, I repeat, if the principle is sound put it into effect where nine millions of people will get the benefit, and not three and a half or four millions. speechtext:
They at last admit the
fighting ground is now clearly defined, and I am glad of it. I am glad that the line of cleavage between us is distinct and well defined, and that we have a platform upon which we can fight and appeal with confidence to the public. I am one of those who believe with Aristotle when he said "One man's privilege ends where the other man's rights begin." Hon. gentlemen opposite are the party of the privileged classes. We of the rest of the House are the supporters of the idea that every man should stand in an equal position before the government of the country. The ex-Minister of Finance when he was speaking on the budget the other day talked of paying due regard to the labouring interests and the interests of the producers of Canada. But what would happen if the producers of the Dominion were to come and ask the protectionist manufacturers of the country-those who are now enjoying the benefit of a protective tariff-to bonus the farmer for every head of live stock or every bushel of wheat he produced. What a howl would go up if such a request were preferred, and yet that is exactly the kind of claim my hon. friends opposite are advancing at the present time. My hon. friends make no attempt to disguise the nature of their request.

The Budget-Mr. Cahill
They are quite frank in asking on behalf of the protected interests to be allowed to coin profits from the tax payers of this country. I remember reading when Mussolini came into power in Italy that one of his first acts was to banish the professional beggars from Rome. If Mussolini were in this country to-day one of his first acts would be to banish the class of supplicants to which I refer. I have no quarrel with those who honestly believe that protection is a good thing. Doubtless there are many in this country who hold that view; but if I were to make profits from an industry in this country that could only exist under a system of protection I should consider myself dishonest. I should not consider I was getting my money honestly if I could not make a living out of an enterprise capable of standing on its own footing without the slightest assistance from the tax payers of this country. I a.m satisfied that many manufacturers do not view the question in that light, that even the leader of the opposition does not take that view, but that is the way it appeals to me. If a manufacturer cannot conduct his business without it being bolstered up by the money of the tax payers it is a case of others submitting to taxation for his benefit, and that is certainly not right conduct on the part of a citizen of any country.
The hon. member for West York referred to the labouring man in the Maritime provinces and to the wheat grower in the West. Take the case of a fisherman returning from the Grand banks to his home in Lunenburg with a cargo of fish. What would he think if, after going into the Boston market and selling his fish there, he had to give a portion of his gain from that sale to bolster up a plough manufacturer in Hamilton or some other place in Ontario. What benefit to the fisherman of the Maritime provinces would there be in such a policy as that? Or what encouragement or profit can a farmer who is growing wheat in Alberta and shipping it to Vancouver and from there to Liverpool derive from the fact that he had to pay a few more dollars for a binder in order to give protection to a manufacturer in Toronto or elsewhere in Canada? Such an argument is not reasonable or sound. It is a fact, that the customs duties in the past have been regarded as an easy way of collecting taxation.

My hon. friends are attempting to make a great cry out of the fact that there is an emigration movement from this country. They talk about the expenditures for the war. Why after the war was over they spent money with a free hand. They built a merchant marine at a cost of some sixty or seventy million dollars. They made loans to Roumania and other European countries. We told them at the time that they might never expect to get a cent of it back, and they have not. They went on expending money in that way, and they are now criticizing the government for not reducing taxation, balancing the budget the first year after they came into power, or doing all kinds of things they never expected or hoped to do or never attempted to do when they were collecting the taxation during the time of inflated business in the var period and the immediate period after the war.

speechtext: The hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) told the House that this budget was prepared for the purpose of catching the Progressive vote.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
My right hon. friend says
"hear, hear." I remember he applauded that idea. It also catches the votes on this side of the House, and it will probably catch a vote of a majority in the neighbourhood of a hundred over my hon. friend's party. If we should go to the country, and if the members of the Progressive party and the members on this side of the House are good judges of the feelings of their constituents and their desires it should catch the same proportion in the country. That is the quarrel my hon. friend has uTith the budget. It is not what he -wants; far from it. But he will hope to succeed with the assistance of practically all the great organizations of this country at his back, because he will practically have the railway corporation, the banking institutions, the press of the country and all the special interests and specially priviliged people at his back, trying to fool the electors of this country again as they did in 1911. But it will probably take the people a few years yet to forget, and they will not have forgotten by the time the next election takes place, nor is it likely they will forget the administration of my right hon. friend till doomsday. After the election of 1896 the Liberal party remained in power for fifteen years, and it is probable that their present tenure of office will be longer than that.
It is wise for the government to practise economy. I do not believe in a government attempting to do all the business of a country. I think the government should practise
The Budget-Mr. Cahill

economy in their expenditure and reduce taxation as much as possible, in order to allow business to develop. The people will take care of the business enterprises if the government will look after purely governmental matters. I am tempted to quote from Macaulay a few words which appealed to me as one of the best political platforms for the Liberal part,}' that I know of. He said:
Our rulers will best promote the improvement of the nation by strictly confining themselves to their own legitimate duties, by leaving capital to find its most lucrative course, commodities their fair price, industry and intelligence their natural reward, idleness and folly their natural punishment ; by maintaining peace, by defending property, by diminishing the price of law, and by observing strict economy in every department of the state.' Let the government do this: the people will assuredly do the rest.
If my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and his party had followed that policy this country to-day would not be
10 p.m. loaded with responsibility with which they are burdened. Far from it. We would have been in a much better position, and the country would have been back to that condition of prosperity which it enjoyed during the time of the previous Liberal administration, when the party tried to leave private business in the hands of private corporations. That, after all, is the best policy for any country, especially a young country.
I do not think the exodus from Canada to the United States is altogether due to the high taxation that has been necessary for the last year or two. I think our banking system is organized on a wrong basis for the development of this country. I hope we will be able to work out something in the Banking and Commerce committee that will give us a better banking system for the people. The present system is merely one for gathering, in numerous branches throughout the country, moneys to be devoted to investments at the head offices, which happen to be in the cities of Montreal and Toronto. This system does not make for a balanced development of the country. I believe that has as much to do with people leaving the country as has the tariff.
Another thing that I believe will have to be adjusted before we get any great volume of immigrants to this country is our naturalization policy. The principle of an immigrant's forswearing allegiance to his former state and swearing allegiance to the government of the country of his adoption is a relic of European conditions under which it was necessary for a man to pledge himself during his lifetime to fight the battles of the country into which he moved. For example, if a man moved

from Belgium to France, or from France to German}', the government naturally expected him to forswear his allegiance to his native country, because he would be required to shoulder arms in the near future in defence of his adopted land. That is absolutely unnecessary in this country. I think that we should have a simple system whereby an immigrant would declare his allegiance to Canada without being obliged to do something that is so distasteful to many people who come here. Forswearing one's allegiance is something that has no particular significance to tiie native-born Canadian inasmuch as he is never called upon to comply with any such painful obligation; but it does mean a great deal indeed to the immigrant who comes here. Something therefore should be done in this direction to facilitate the entry of immigrants into Canada.
In conclusion, I would observe that the budget is one that lends encouragement to the country generally, and I believe that it has been accepted throughout the length and breadth of the land. And if by any chance the government should deem it necessary to go to the country at this time I am convinced that they would come back very much stronger than they are to-day and much stronger than both of the parties combined who are expected to support the budget that is at present under consideration.

speechtext: I understood, Mr. Speaker, that the arrangement was that I should speak on the budget to-night. Evidently there has been a misunderstanding, and I would ask the hon. member to withdraw his motion.
