speechtext: I have no objection to doing so; I withdraw the motion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
In common with you, Mr. Speaker, and every other hon. member of this House, I regret that on the present occasion I have not had the pleasure of listening to the Minister of Finance himself (Mr. Fielding) in the delivery of the budget speech. It has been my good fortune to have listened to, and supported by my vote in this House, thirteen of the seventeen budget speeches that have been delivered by that hon. gentleman, and while I shall not attempt to eulogize him in the presence of hon. members who have seen him

The Budyet-Air. Marcil (Bonaventure)
discharge his responsible duties as Minister of Finance in this House, I do desire to say a word or two in regard to my own personal experience with him. I had the pleasure of being in that part of Canada where he is best known, having had an opportunity at two general elections, in 1908 and 1911, of accompanying the Minister of Finance through the Maritime provinces where I witnessed the prestige and general confidence which he inspired in these three provinces by the sea. His record as provincial premier was behind him and his work as Minister of Finance in Canada was then meeting with success, to the general satisfaction and advantage of this country. I hope that Providence will spare him to return to us to continue the good work that he has done; for a man who has given forty years of his life to the service of his country cannot easily be dispensed with without a great loss all round.
It was also my good fortune to hear, with pleasure and approval, the present budget speech delivered by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). I have known the Acting Minister of Finance for some time; he represents the combined constituencies of Chateauguay-Huntingdon, an ideal combination of English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians. These constituencies have been represented in this House in the past by some distinguished men, to mention only the late Hon. Mr. Holton and Mr. Julius Scriver, two of the most distinguished members of the Liberal party hailing from the province of Quebec in the old days. The Acting Minister of Finance has worthily stepped into their place and is performing his duties in his present responsible position quite satisfactorily. As a man who has listened to various speeches in this House during many years, I wish to congratulate him on his performance, \nd more particularly on the brevity of his peech; and I hope that in the budget speech cf this year a record has been established which public men in Canada will emulate. The shorter a speech is the more effective it becomes. For many years in Great Britain, in the mother of parliaments, the budget speech has invariably been delivered in about an hour, and some of the greatest orations of Gladstone and other eminent statesmen have been delivered within that space of time. I trust that the example which the hon. the Acting Minister has set will be followed by all; and with that end in view I do not intend to speak at great length this evening. I think it is my duty however.
both to my constituents and to the people of the country at large, that I should refer to the budget to some extent. The keynote of the budget is, in a few words, the development of Canadian basic industries. The concluding paragraph of the speech of the Acting Minister of Finance defines the policy of the present government, which I know will have the support of the immense majority in this House and the equally immense majority of the country on the first occasion that presents itself for the demonstration of the confidence of the people in the administration. The words of the Acting Minister to which I refer are:
Whatever division of opinion Canadians may have, surely we share a united confidence in the future of our country. We have great natural resources. We have certain basic industries, upon the success of which, depend the growth of all other industries, the greater development of our trade. Of these basic industries, I would place agriculture, in all its varied branches, first. Next to agriculture, I would place our forests, our minerals and our fisheries. A real national policy is a policy that will encourage the growth and development of these basic industries. The more of the products of the farm, the fisheries, the mines and the forest we have going to market, the greater will be the earnings of our transportation companies-the greater the purchasing power of the nation and as a consequence we shall have factories running full time and tradesmen working overtime to supply the needs of those who will have money to buy. In that belief, Sir, we submit to-day proposals to lighten the burden of taxation on these primary, basic industries. Our budget shows a reduction in debt of $30,000,000 last year, and a reduction in taxation of $24,000,000 this year. It is confidently expected that this reduction will give such impetus to trade that it will result in greater development and prosperity to all the provinces of Canada.
I regret having had to -read an extract from a speech that is still so fresh in the minds of all hon. gentlemen, but I have done so because it epitomises in a few lines the precise policy of the present administration which, as far as I understand, is in keeping with the policy of the Liberal party as enunciated in convention in 1919. The four foundation stones of national prosperity are agriculture, the forests, the fisheries and the mines; and without the prosperity of these four great branches of industry no prosperity is possible in any other direction. We may venture to foster and to encourage the manufacture of anything under the sun, and we may attempt to compete with the Americans, with the French, with the English or with any other manufacturing nation. But we shall never attain success in any branch of manufacturing unless these four basic industries are prosperous in this country.
The hon. minister has faced a problem that was well-nigh overwhelming. Older members of this House and you, Mr. Speaker, will
1404	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure)
remember when we had to gather but $18,000,000 a year to meet the interest charges on a public debt of only $350,000,000. That is long, long since. Now we have to face conditions that are almost overwhelming compared with what they were in the old days. But the Canadian people are equal to the task. They have already accomplished what has never been surpassed by any other nation in the world. Therefore I am confident that with the working out of this policy and with proper legislative encouragement which will keep our people at home and attract newcomers-immigrants who will be willing to share our burdens and to abide by our laws and constitution, thus becoming good Canadians-the future of Canada is as bright as it ever was. In fact the position of this country is to-day the best in the world, for we are free from many of the disturbing questions which trouble many other countries, and which we hope will never arise here. As Canadians, regardless of provincial boundaries, come together and get to know each other better, so will all our difficulties be overcome, and we shall be able to build up on this North American continent a nation of which we and our descendants may be truly proud.
The Acting Minister of Finance is a Scotsman in origin, and therefore a very prudent man in dealing with money matters. After giving us this great relief of decreasing our public debt to the extent of $30,000,000 and reducing our taxation by $24,000,000. he turned to the fiscal year 1924-25 and said:
T come now to the fiscal year 1924-25. Estimates of revenue for the year upon which we have just entered cannot be made with any degree of accuracy. The revenue we would receive on the present basis of taxation wbuld be materially affected by reductions in taxes which, in view of the most satisfactory out-come of the year just closed, it is proposed to submit to parliament. It is hoped, however, to offset any considerable reduction in the revenue by a most rigid economy in expenditures. The estimates now before the House show a very substantial reduction as compared with the estimates of last year. We shall no doubt have supplementaries, but rigid economy will be exercised in their preparation; and in this the government hopes for and expects co-operation from all sections of Canada.
For my part, Mr. Speaker, I am willing by speech and by vote to support any proposal that will tend to do away with waste and extravagance. But there is such a thing as productive expenditure, and I am going to call the attention of the government and the House to an expenditure of this class, not because it happens to be in my own constituency, for I am sure there must be many similar cases in the rest of the Dominion, but because such productive expenditure is necessary to help us meet our obligations. There

is no doubt that we must increase our population, and the most effective way to do so is to keep our people at home; this means that we must give them employment; to give them employment we must develop our resources, and to develop our resources the public moneys have on certain occasions to be brought into profitable and effective use. There are in my constituency, Mr. Speaker, as you are aware, large timber limits covering thousands of square miles. The country is barely developed, but on the seashore there is considerable settlement. In the centre of my constituency the Bathurst Lumber Company own five hundred square miles of timber limits formerly the property of Lieutenant Governor Robitaille. The outlet for these limits is on the Bonaventure river, practically half-way between Gaspe and Campbellton, the only deep water ports we have on the bay of Chaleur. In the old days the company had at its head the late Senator Edwards and other capitalists of these parts who established mills at Bonaventure and New Richmond, giving employment to several hundred men. For more than ten years under very trying circumstances they operated the mills but what with defective railway facilities, due to shortage of motive power and rolling stock, and lack of any deep water port on a shore line of 200 miles, they finally had to close them down. As a result the population of Bonaventure has decreased by eight hundred, and the mayor writes me that fifty families are preparing to leave in the spring for other parts of Canada or for the United States. There has been an exodus from Gaspe and Bonaventure, largely owing to the fact that we have lost our industries for want of effective means of transportation by rail and by water. The Bathurst Lumber Company, as my friends from the Maritime provinces know, is one of the soundest and most enterprising corporations in that part of the Cominion. At the present time they have a large industry at Bathurst, and to keep it in operation they have to cut their timber in Bonaventure and raft it 25 miles across the bay of Chaleur to Bathurst, where they are served by the Intercolonial railway. Consequently the people of my constituency lose the work of converting the timber into lumber, and have to go away to seek work, while our farmers are deprived of any home market and agriculture is decreasing every year.
What has happened to the Bathurst Lumber Company has also happened to the Province of Quebec Lumber Association, which owns large timber limits in the county. They moved across the bay to Dalhousie, and they are

The Budget-Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure)
rafting their timber over to this mill, with the result that the men living in the vicinity of the timber limits are left without employment. In the county which you, Mr. Speaker, have the honour to represent we have a large pulp mill at Chandler which was erected some years ago by capitalists from Philadelphia, but to-day it is owned largely by Canadians. They have to export their product down to Gaspe to find a deep water terminus, having no shipping facilities of any kind, and therefore the place is seriously handicapped.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and that of the House, I wish to lay these concrete proposals before the government as they have already been laid before the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) by the Bathurst Lumber Company. The directors of that company say: Give us increased harbour facilities at Bonaventure. It will cost you $200,000 according to the estimates of last year. It will take at least four years to spend that sum of money, but if the government are prepared to do that, we are prepared to spend $300,000 on our own part, and the result will be the building up of an industry that will employ three or four hundred men. In order that the matter may be better understood I would like to have the privilege of reading a letter sent by Mr. McLean, president of the company, to the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. King). It reads as follows:
August 14, 1923.
Dear Mr. King:-
The people of Bonaventure, Quebec, have been requesting us for some time to start an industry at Bonaventure for manufacturing at least a portion of the timber that we are now cutting on the Gaspe peninsula at that point and we had a meeting there two weeks ago at which a very large number of the residents of Bonaventure were present and resolutions were passed at this meeting, copies of which I understand the Hon. Chas. Marcil has forwarded to you. The position is as follows: We are prepared to put in a good, substantial plant there for manufacturing providing we can obtain the necessary facilities to make a success of our enterprise, and in order to do this it will be necessary that we should have a protected harbour and dredging done so that sea-going vessels could go into the harbour and lie in safe protection. In addition to this, of course, we will have to have railway facilities but this is something that we can easily arrange outside of the harbour improvements required. We have agreed with the people of Bonaventure that we will proceed to put in this plant providing they can succeed in getting their harbour improvements made, and as they are desirous of having this done at the earliest possible moment in order that our construction work may begin there, we wish to add our plea for this work being done. Under the circumstances if you could arrange to have a survey made and ascertain what is necessary to make this a good shipping port where vessels could take cargo on or discharge cargo during a period of seven or eight months of the year, we would like very much to see this survey made. You probably know that Bonaventure is about half way between Matapedia
and Gaspe and it is the only available port on that whole coast where a deep water harbour is possible and as it so centrally located and also is at the mouth of the important Bonaventure river, where there are large quantities of wood, there is no reason why this could not be made a very important shipping port for that whole coast as well as a point where materials of all kinds could go in and be loaded on board cars for distribution to that whole district. We simply want to add our request to that of the people of Bonaventure to have this work done at as early a date as possible and we are prepared to proceed with our enterprise and give business for shipping so that the port would justify the expense of making the harbour.
Thanking you for your consideration.
Yours very truly,
Angus McLean,
President.
That was the proposal that was made to the minister at a time when he and his colleagues were striving to practise the most rigid economy. At first glance they felt it necessary to turn down the proposal, as they had been obliged to turn down many others relating to other parts of Canada. But I make a special plea in' favour of this one, for several reasons. In the first place, we are isolated from the large centres. We are 600 miles from Montreal, and we have a very inefficient railway service. We have a hard country to live in, because of the long winter season. It is a part of Canada in which very few immigrants from Europe will ever settle; they generally go to the Eastern townships, to Ontario or to the West, and not one in a thousand would dream of locating in the Gaspe district. We have a population born in the place; the people have lived there for generations, and it is in the interests of the country that these young people, who are ideal axemen, ideal men for the lumber camps and the lumbering industry, for the deep sea fishing we have on the coast and for agriculture as well, should be given employment and kept at home.
The minister, in response to the resolution that was sent to him, adopted at a public meeting held at Bonaventure on the first of August, presided over by Monseigneur Matte Vicar General of the new see of Gaspe, kindly sent down an engineer to make a very thorough survey of the whole situation, especially in view of the fact that under the Laurier administration $100,000 had been expended at Bonaventure for the purpose of creating a harbour and building a breakwater. But it is needless to say that from 1911 until 1921 nothing whatever was done; the work was abandoned and these industries moved away. The question is this:	Can Canada
afford to lose this population? Can Canada afford to lose this industry? Can Canada afford the $100,000 that has already been ex-

1406	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure)
pended?-because that expenditure has not resulted in deepening the harbour as it would be deepened by the extension of this breakwater and by deepening the basin as asked for. The report of the engineer is typical of conditions in many parts of eastern Quebec and, I believe, in the Maritime provinces. Our friends in Ontario and in the West do not have to contend with the sea; they are not familiar with these conditions, and I have no doubt that when they hear this report they will have some idea of the importance of this matter to the people living down by the sea, people who, as I have said, live under difficult conditions, far removed from the thickly settled portions of Canada. This is the report of the engineer:
Department of Public Works,
District Engineer's Office, Rimouski, P.Q., Oct. 25, 1923.
Sir:-
With reference to your telegram of Oct. 17th, and to your letter of Aug. 10th ult., re file P.Q. 36, in regard to harbour improvements which are being requested at Bonaventure river, County of Bonaventure, P.Q., I beg to submit the following.
Bonaventure river or St. Bonaventure, in the county of the same name, is situated on the north shore of the Baie des Chaleurs, 10 miles west from New Carlisle and 90 miles east from Matapedia. It is the largest village of the county; lumbering, farming and fishing are extensive. The fish export firm of Robin Jones & Whitman has a large establishment at that place, which is also a distribution centre; all kind of farm and dairy produce, cattle, etc., are yearly exported; several thousand cords of pulpwood are cut in the vicinity and shipped through this point.
In addition to this local traffic, the Bathurst Lumber Co., Limited, owns, on the westerly shore of the mouth of the Bonaventure river, flowing into the sea, through the easterly portion of the village, large saw, shingle and planing mills, which have been left vacant and idle during the last ten years, due to the fact that the annual timber cut done in their Bonaventure river limits was being rafted to Bathurst, N.B., to be milled in the company's plant at that place.
The annual cut of timber done by the Bathurst Co., in their limits of the Bonaventure river (about 500 sq. miles) approximates 20,000,000 ft. B.M. of lumber; approximately 10 to 15 million feet are also taken out of the Little Cascapedia river, the mouth of which is located about 20 miles west from Bonaventure river.
It is evident that this rafting over the New Brunswick of the lumber cut in the Bonaventure county means a serious loss to the local industry and traffic.
It is now proposed, however, as stated by Mr. McLean, president of the Bathurst Lumber Co., that the said company make at Bonaventure village the centre of their milling operations in the region: they will consequently reopen their mills, enlarge them if necessary to ensure employment to at least 300 men: the company stands prepared to an outlay of $300,000 to modernize the existing saw-mills, and to build a pulp rossing mill as promised to the population of Bonaventure, during the meeting held at that place on August 1, by the head of the Bathurst Lumber Co., Mr. McLean.
But all this industrial boom will take place only if the necessary shipping accommodation and harbour facilities are provided, permitting ocean-going freighters and steam barges to load and unload from a

wharf which should be built at that place with sufficient depth of water to allow safe navigation in the harbour: a deep water harbour has consequently to be found or created in the vicinity of the mouth of Bonaventure river.
In regard to deep water harbours, allow me to call your attention to the fact that the whole of this region of eastern Quebec lies as yet only partly developed, owing to the lack of transport facilities: there is only one railroad in both counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe operating from Matapedia to Gaspe, a distance of 202 miles, only one passenger train and one freight train a day. Moreover, owing to the bad condition of the road-bed, only very light cars are hauled so that the traffic is very poorly accommodated; consequently to relieve congestion of travelling and freight hauling, transportation by water should be resorted to. Unfortunately nature has not favoured most of the localities along this coast with natural facilities; harbours there are a-plenty but, in practically all of them the water is shallow and, with very few exceptions, unless they are improved, they do not afford the required accommodation.
Bonaventure river is located approximately half way between Gaspe and Matapedia and should be, from this geographical location, the commercial and industrial centre of the region. In former times, before 1914, such a condition was existing, and Bonaventure was enjoying a prosperous trade and traffic which would certainly be resumed with the revival of industry as above outlined.
With deep water harbour facilities at Bonaventure, this place should become a business centre of large importance. It would be the meeting place of both ends of the Gaspe peninsula and become the principal' timber market place of the region.
To meet the requirements such as described by the interested parties during the meeting held at Bonaventure. I consider that, in order not to have the expenditure already incurred by the department in the locality wasted, the existing training pier should be extended 1,000 feet in length by 20 feet in width in a straight direction, and 600 feet in length by 30 feet in width in a south direction: a basin along the easterly side of the 30-foot wide portion of the wharf should also be dredged as shown on accompanying plan.
The construction of the above-mentioned extension 1,600 feet in length by 20 feet and 30 feet in width would cost approximately $145,000; the dredging of a basin averaging 1,040 feet in length by 300 feet in width to 16 feet L.W.S.T., would involve the removal of approximately 68,000 cubic yards of material, measured in place, which at 50 cents per cubic yard would cost $34,000.
No borings have been taken out in vicinity, but I am of the opinion that the dredging can be done without meeting with considerable hardships.
The whole cost of the requested and described improvements should be approximately, including cost of necessary contingencies, $190,000.
Yours obediently,
P. E. Amiot,
District Engineer.
A similar letter was forwarded to the right hon. the Prime Minister, and I have no doubt that he will give the matter proper consideration when it is taken up in council. Here is the situation:	Even if a small
amount were granted in the supplementary estimates of say $25,000 or thereabouts, to commence this work, not one dollar of that money could be spent before next winter because the timber has to be taken out of

The Budget-Mr. Marcil (Bonaventure)
the forests and hauled down to the seashore, so the work practically would not begin until the spring of 1925. They could only do a certain amount of work each year, and this expenditure of $200,000 would cover certainly a period of two or three years, if not four, which would mean a spread of the expenditure. I am not asking for this amount to be spent in one year. The Bathurst Lumber Company spent this year $40,000 there in the construction of piers and booms for the distribution of their logs and to carry on their operations.
I hope I shall have the indulgence of this House for having brought this matter up, but I think I am giving expression to the feeling not only of the government but of many members in this House when I say that in applying rigid economy we must not go too far. We must not cut out what, as in this case, we might call productive expenditure. Whenever a reasonable proposition or a concrete proposal is made by a solvent corporation, when the work is already under way, when a large amount of money has already been expended, when the limits are there, when the resources are there, when the people exploiting them have undoubted capital, when their standing is of the first order, I think, Mr. Speaker, it would be false economy on the part of the Canadian government to turn down an offer such as this or to turn down any offer which would give an opportunity to develop our resources and give employment to our people and keep them at home. '
This question of carrying our lumber over into another province is not a new one. It has been discussed many times in the Quebec legislature. It has been brought up on several occasions by Hon. John Hall Kelly, now solicitor for the Lumber Association, and by Mr. Bugeaud, late member for Bonaventure and now on the bench, but the answer of the Quebec government was always this, that the clause in the British North America Act which prevents any barriers being placed against interprovincial trade applies to lumber as to everything else. Along the Ottawa river practically all the mills in this province are kept going by timber from the province of Quebec, and the same thing is true of New Brunswick to-day. The lumber manufactured in New Brunswick is brought over from the province of Quebec. I do not object to the prosperity of New Brunswick at all. I am advocating at the present time, and will continue to advocate, a closer relationship between Quebec and New Brunswick at that point, because our people from the province of 90i
Quebec and from New Brunswick are becoming more and more allied every day. There is an invasion of New Brunswick by Quebec, and I hope that the old settlers of the province of New Brunswick will stay at home and not be attracted by the lure of the west or of the United States, because some day they may find another Quebec in the province of New Brunswick. The French-Canadians are going into New Brunswick because they have an opportunity there; they have faith in that province, and I would like to see the old settlers of New Brunswick stay in that province rather than leave for the United States or the West.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to say one last word in support of this proposal, and to ask the government to give it fair consideration. I think I have advanced arguments which cannot easily be refuted. They speak for keeping the people at home, for giving them employment, for developing our resources, and the moment the government have the necessary guarantees I hope they will find their way, notwithstanding the wise caution given by the Acting Minister of Finance, to at least complete this work so that we shall be able to keep our people at home and continue to share in the general prosperity of Canada.
Mr. Hubbs moved the adjournment of the debate.

Before putting the motion I wish to explain, in justice to the hon. member, that being a new member he did not realize he was losing his right to address the House again on this question by withdrawing his motion for the adjournment of the debate, in order that the hon, member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) might have an opportunity of speaking. According to May and Bourinot the House in such a case is generally very indulgent, and I hope that the hon. gentleman may not lose his right to address the House on this question. Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member shall have leave to address the House in this debate and now move its adjournment?
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

maintopic: INTERPARLIAMENTARY UNION. INVITATION TO MEET IN WASHINGTON IN 1925
INTERPARLIAMENTARY UNION. INVITATION TO MEET IN WASHINGTON IN 1925
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received from the Acting Under Secretary of State for External Affairs the following letter:
Ottawa, 14th April, 1924.
Sir,-I have the honour to transmit, herewith, copy of a letter which has been received from the agent of this department at Washington, D.C., United States, en-

Interparliamentary Union
closing copies of H. J. Res. 204, requesting the President to invite the Interparliamentary Union to meet in Washington City in 1925, and authorizing an appropriation to defray the expenses of the meeting, together with copies of Report No. 475 on the above bill.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Signed) W. H. Walker.
Acting Under-Secretary of State
for External Affairs.
The Speaker of the House of Commons,
Ottawa.
. The resolution adopted by the House of Representatives reads as follows:
In the House of Representatives March 3, 1924
Mr. Temple introduced the following joint resolution; which was referred to the Committee on Foreign Affairs and ordered to be printed
April 8, 1924
Reported with amendments, committed to the committee of the Whole House on the state of the Union, and ordered to be printed.
Joint Resolution
Requesting the President to invite the Interparliamentary Union to meet in Washington City in 1925, and authorizing an appropriation to defray the expenses of the meeting.
Whereas the Congress, in an act approved June 30, 1914, requested the President to extend an invitation to the Interparliamentary Union to hold its annual meeting for the year 1915 in the city of Washington, and in the same act appropriated the sum of $40,000 to defray the expenses of the said meeting; and Whereas when the World War led to repeated postponements of the said meeting the Congress repeatedly extended the appropriation: first, the act of July 1, 1916 extended it and made it available for the calendar years 1916 and 1917; second, the act of March 3rd, 1917, extended the appropriation and made it available for the calendar year 1918; third, the act of April 15, 1918, extended the appropriation and made it available for the calendar year 1919; and Whereas this appropriation repeatedly extended has lapsed, no part of it having been expended, and the meeting thus arranged for in the city of Washington has not been held; Therefore be it Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That the President be requested to invite the Interparliamentary Union to hold its annual meeting for the year 1925 in the city of Washington.
Sec. 2. That for the purpose of defraying the expenses incident to said meeting the appropriation of $50,000, to be expended under such rules and regulations as the Secretary of State may prescribe, is hereby authorized.
I thought I should read that resolution which has been sent to me by the Under Secretary of State for External Affairs because many members of the House of Commons as well as of the Senate are members of the Interparliamentary Union.

Before moving the adjournment of the House I wish to

mention to hon. members that to-morrow I propose to move that the resolution passed providing for an Easter adjournment until the 22nd' instant, be rescinded, and that the date for reassembling after the recess be fixed for April 24th, instead of April 22nd, should the House give unanimous consent. I may say that one of the reasons for making the motion is that the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have extended an invitation to hon. members from the West to visit, the Maritime provinces during the Easter vacation. A large number of hon. gentlemen are taking advantage of the invitation so extended but the time we have agreed upon will allow them scarcely any time to inspect objects of interest. I may add that the government itself would welcome two days' extension of the recess if the House is unanimous in its favour. I now move that the House adjourn.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 10.45 p.m.
